questions.prompt: Rock particles or mineral matter This is a non - living matter that makes up 45% of the soil volume. The size of the soil particles varies from a diameter of 2mm in gravel to less than 0.002mm in clay soil.

questions.prompt: Organic matter About 5% of the soil volume consists of organic matter made up of decomposing plants and animal and also living organisms. Soils with dark brown colour indicate that it contains a lot of humus .

questions.prompt: This occupies the space between the soil particles. It is made up of 25% soil volume. Air mainly consists of nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide as well as other small gases. Soils with large particles have more air spaces compared to soils with sm aller particles.

questions.prompt: Water Water occupies the space between rock particles making up 25% of soil volume. After heavy rains there will be more water in the soil, while after a dry period there will be much less. @TZ 14 of 14 INVESTIGATING SOIL CONSTITUENTS Experiment 1  Finding out if the soil has inorganic matter - Collect dry sample of soil - Spread it on a sheet of paper and study it carefully  What do you see?  You will the see the particles of broken down rocks.  This is the solid part of soil call ed inorganic matter Experiment 2  Finding out if the soil has organic matter - Collect a dry sample of soil - Put the dry sample in a bottle with a lid - Fill up the bottle with water and close it - Shake the bottle for a few minutes - Allow the bottle to stand for at least 15 minutes.  You will see some materials will float at the top of the water  These materials are referred to as organic matter Experiment 3  Finding out if soil is made up of water - Put a small amount of dry soil in a dry bottle and close the b ottle tightly with a lid - Heat the soil in the bottle slowly on a fire. - Observe the bottle after at least 20 minutes  You will see water droplets inside the bottle  The droplets of water shows the presence of water in the soil Experiment 4  Finding out if soil has air - Collect dry soil in the bottle - Half fill the bottle with water  You will see air bubbles rising from the soil  This shows the presence of air in the soil

questions.prompt: Thinning - removing extra and weak seedlings so that those that remain in the bed are not crowded.  So that remaining seedlings can have enough space.  To reduce completion between the growing seedlings.  To enhance yield as the remaining crops will grow well.  It can be done using hands.
questions.explanation: Agriculture (Grade 5): Award 1 mark(s) for demonstrating required syllabus competence.

grading_criteria: Award 1 mark(s) for demonstrating required syllabus competence.

questions.prompt: Prunning - Getting rid of dead and unproductive plant parts which are useful or productive.  So that healthy and productive plant parts remain .  Enhance growth of the plant.  So that food, water and air are not wasted on dead and unproductive plant parts.  Can be don e to certain plants which are used to decorate.  A very sharp knife, a scissor can be used. @TZ 9 of 14

questions.prompt: Pest and disease control - chemicals such pesticides ( for killing pests ) and weedicides/herbicides ( for killing weeds ) can be used.  If not controlled plants will gr ow poorly and eventually die.  Pest and diseases cause poor yield.  We get poor crop quality from plants attacked by pests and diseases.  A knap sack sprayer is used to apply the chemicals.

questions.prompt: Weed ing - The removal of unwanted plants in the plot. The unwanted plants are called .  Weeds compete with crops for space, water, food, air and sunlight making crops grow poorly.  Weeds spread disease and pest to plant which might end up killing them.  They reduce yield as the plants will grow poorly.

questions.prompt: Gapping - Filling in gaps left by plants which either do not germinate or dried out  To increase yield.  This can reduce spoilage  improve quality and ensure that you have the best quality produce for your customers METHODS OF PRESERVING VEGETABLE  Vegetables are very perishable; therefore, they need to be preserved. o Preserving vegetables means protecting them getting damaged or spoilt easily.  If vegetables are preserved : - they will last longer. - they will be available throughout the year - they will not lose nutrients. Vegetables can be preserved in the followin g ways:
options: Dehydration - Removing moisture from vegetable or drying them. - Vegetables are left in the sun after harvesting so that moisture can be removed. A lot of vegetables can be dried such onions, spinach, bean leaves, pig weed, cochorus etc. - When moisture has been removed from vegetables, micro - organisms such as bacteria will not grow. Micro - organisms cause vegetables to rot.

Refrigeration - Keeping vegetables in a refrigerator (fridge) where temperatures are very low to preserve them. A cold environment slows the growth of micro - organisms hence vegetables can be stored a longer periods of time. A lot of vegetables can be refrigerated such as : - Plums - Peaches - Apple - Grape - Mango - Apricot - Raisins @TZ 10 of 14

Freezing - Putting vegetables in f reezer where temperatures are extremely cold . - There will be no micro - organisms and vegetables can be stored for a very long, long time. Most vegetables can be refrigerated such: strawberry

Canning - This involves cleaning, slicing and putting them in can s. - Fruits that can be canned include: Pears - Pineapple - Guava - Peaches VEGETABLE FARM RECORDS  If the information is about what was bought or sold, costs and profit or loss, the n it is called a financial record .  If the information is about important things or events that have taken place in the garden when growing vegetables, then it is called a diary record .  If the information kept is showing the quantity of the vegetable crop harvested , then it is called production record.

questions.prompt: A dry pot can be dipped into paint or a colo ured slip. Rolling out slabs Joining slabs together CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 14 Burnishing clay products This means applying or rubbing polish, wax, paint or anything on the surface of hard clay product to make it shiny. Firing clay This means baking pottery products in a special oven called a kiln at high temperatures before using it. Firing makes clay hard and strong. Burnishe d clay jar F ired clay pot CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 15 Embroidery stitches Embroidery is an art of using stiches in a creative way to decorate clothing and household items. Below are examples of embroidery stitches: Chain stitch satin stitch Stem stitch CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 16 Embroidery hand stiches applied on a project Cross stitch step by Herringbone stitch step by CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 17 Seams A seam is a line of stitches that join two pieces of fabric. In sewing, a seam is the join where two or more layers of fabric or other materials are held together with stitches. Types of seams a) Open seam / plain seam It is used if you are sewing a fabric which does not fray easily and if the seam does not have to be very strong. b) French seam It is useful for fabrics that fray easily. It is stronger than that an open seam but cannot be used on a fabric that is very thick. CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 18 c) Flat - fell seam It is used for clothing that is won next to the skin. It is often used on the side seams of jeans. It leaves a line of stitches visible on the outside of the garment. MECHANISMS Mechanisms A system or structure of moving parts in a machine that performs some function . Mechanisms movements There are four main types of movements that mechanisms can produce. CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 19 LINEAR MOTION linear motion is anything that moves in a straight line . It is represented by and arrow. RECIPROCATING MOTION It is a repetitive up - and - down or back - and - forth linear motion. It is represented both a line with arrows on both ends. Example include sewing machine needle, pump engines, cutting blade etc. ROTARY MOTION Rotary motion is anything that moves in a circle. Think of a spinning wheel bicycle wheel. The movement is represented by a n open circle with an arrow. OSCILLATING MOTION Something that oscillates moves back and forth like a swing for ming an arc . It is represented by curved line with two arrow heads. This type of motion is found everywhere in our world: a sprinkler system and the pendulum of a clock . CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 20 Crank mechanisms A cran k is a mechanism that is used to turn or apply rotary motion to a shaft. An example of crank mechanism is the pedals o f a bicycle . The input and output of a crank mechanism The input force is the force that is applied for example pedalling a bicycle in a rotary motion. The output force is the motion the mechanism produces for example when the bicycle moves forward in a linear motion. The mechanical advantage of crank mechanism • Crank mechanism makes us to do heavy work with less effort . • They change one type of motion to another e ., rotary to linear like in a moving bicycle. CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 21 Cam and follower mechanism A cam and follower change rotary motion into reciprocating motion. Do this, when a cam turns, it pushes the follower up and down . The diagram below shows how a cam works. A cam can be a wheel with irregular shape . The follower is a bar designed to follow the shape of the cam. TYPES OF CAMS There are different types of cams , with different shapes. The shape makes the follower moves in different ways. The types of cams incl ude p ear, eccentric or circular, heart and drop and others. CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 22 The input and output of cam and follower. CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 23 CUTTING AND SHAPING TOOLS o Tenon saw o Coping saw o Hand drill o Twist drill o Bradawl o Smoothing plane o Flat surform o Curved surform o Round surform o Hand file o Half round file o Round file Tenon saw Coping saw Hand drill CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 24 Twist drill Bradawl Smoothing plane CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 25 Flat surfo r m Round surform Flat file Half round file Round file CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 26 FINISHES F inishing is the process of protecting and polishing wooden plastic surfaces which makes its appearance richer and deeper. Types of finishes • P aint • wax • varnish Surface preparation In the process of making products, materials are subjected to a variety of operations such as cutting and drilling. These operations leave behind marks and rough surfaces, thereby spoiling the beauty of the product. Also, such marks may hurt people who use the product. To remove marks and smooth edges and surfaces, we use abrasives. Types of abrasives There are different grades of abrasives, ranging from very coarse to extra fine . Examples of abrasives • Glass paper • Garnet paper • Wet and dry paper • Steel wool Finishing wood  Before applying a finish, you must ensure that your surface is well prepared. This should include the following:  Punch all nails below the surface.  Smooth the surfaces with a smoothing plane.  Smooth the surfaces with glass paper  Fill cr acks or holes with wood filler  Rub down the surfaces with fine glass paper or steel wool  Dust off the surfaces.  Apply appropriate finish such as wax or varnish Finishing edges of acrylic Acrylic sheets usually do require any finish. They already have a goo d surface finish. The edges, however, will have to be smoothed and polished. CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 27 ENTREPRENEURSHIP An entrepreneur is a person who identifies business opportunity, set up a business and run it profitably. The main functions of the entrepreneur are to: • generate new business ideas, recognize business opportunities and determine profitable business ideas. • plan the business and identify the resources required. • bring together and organize resources into a business unit. • take decision on what to produce, how to produce, where to produce and in what amount to produce. • take responsibilities and risks of employing resources of land, labour and capital to produce goods and services. In Botswana entrepreneurs are important because they help the economy in the following ways: • As many people become self - employed there is a meaningful drop in unemployment numbers . • Success is spread among many people. • It is likely that new products and technology will be developed • Job opportunities can be created. • There will be fewer crime and welfare problems. ENTERPRENEURIAL SKILLS Skills of an entrepreneur planning, marketing, organizing, making decisions, interpersonal, leadership, communication etc. Apart from these general skills, there are some skills on which your business can be based, such as drawing and painting, cooking, playing of musical instruments, mending things, singing, dancing, etc. Qualities of an entrepreneur hard working, self - confident, focused, adaptable, honest, healthy, independent, perseverance. Lack of the basic business skills and qualities may lead to business failure. Businesses can also fail because of the following: • The owner do es not know how to run a business • The owner does not know enough about the activities of the business • Lack of management skills • The owner does not keep proper records of transactions CAPA 5 NOTES term 3 - BY Autumn Jeremiah 2023 28 • The business may not be located in the right place • A disaster such as flood or fire can cause a business failure. The entrepreneurial qualities or business skills can be learnt, for example in class. There are also business schools which can help to develop entrepreneurial qualities and skills. The government provide assistant to entrepreneurs who have very bright business ideas but do not have money.

questions.prompt: Rice -------------------------- ( rinse, rise ) TERMS AND TECHNIQUES IN WRITING ALLITERATION Repetition of the same sound at the beginning of two or more words that are next to each other. Examples  Fly away, my fine - feathered friend.  A silvery sliver slid from the needle case. ASSONANCE Vowel rhyme or words that have the same vowel sound. It is often used in poetry. The sl ow ly gr ow ing mighty oa k did shade our h o me for years. CLIMAX The high point of a story. It is followed by an ending called a resolution. DIALOGUE Conversation or talking that takes place between two or more characters. Dialogue is usually enclosed in quotation marks. HYPERBOLE A deliberate exaggeration used as a figure of speech.  My dog is as big as a ten - ton elephant  Their house was so big; you had to drive a car from the front door to the living room. IMAGERY This is creating imaginary pictures using words. This is word painting and these pictures make certain points easier to understand and more interesting to read. Techniques such as allusion , metaphor and simile are examples of imagery.  My dog is very happy ( without imagery)  My dog i s a pig in a mud ( allusion) The boy would not sit down at the desk ( without imagery)  The boy’s desk might as well have been made of pins and needles . (metaphor) METAPHOR A comparison of two different things to show a likeness between them that does not use like or as .  The teacher chimed the roll call.  Peo was drowning in tears after her mother passed away. ONOMATOPOEIA Words that are invented to imitate real sounds. Bang ip, smash, crunch, rip and grrrrr are all examples of onomatopoeia. PARABLE A story with a moral or religious lesson to be learned. Parables are related to fables . PERSONIFICATION This means attributing to things that are not human the personalities and actions of human beings. Feelings can also be personified; for example fear grabbed the victim in its icy clutches . SIMILE A figure of speech that compares two unlike things using the words like or as .  The lion purred like a kitten.  Tshepiso cried as if it were the end of the world.

questions.prompt: ATR - Some parts of harvest were stored to help the poor in times of need. - Majako : when a person helps in the field and then rewarded with part of the harvest. - Mafisa : loaning cattle to the poor so that they help themselves with milk and ploughing. - Molaletsa : a form of cooperation where a people came together to help in doing some field management practices. They were thanked with food and traditional beer. SUMMARY @TZ 11 of 11 Children whose parents are dead are called orphans. Many people and organisations help in taking care of orphans. Orphans are faced with a number of problems such as abuse, not receiving love and misuse of their inheritance. O rphans can be adopted. In their families they feel love, care and acceptance. DESTITUTION  A destitute is a person who does not have money, food, clothes, a place to live and other things needed in life ( people who are very poor ). WAYS IN WHICH INDIVIDUALS SHOULD SHOW CARE FOR DESTITUTES  Traditionally, destitutes were helped through Mafisa, Majako and Molaletsa. Members of the community may help destitutes by:  Giving them donations .  Building them a house .  Employing them .  Teaching them skills whic h they can use to find or create jobs.  Helping protecting their rights.  Protecting them from abuse.  Providing destitutes with services like making their laundry or fetching firewood.  Adopting or helping care for orphans who are destitutes. WAYS IN WHICH T HE GOVERNMENT HELPS DESTITUTES  Registered destitutes are given food rations and food baskets on monthly basis.  They are given money to buy items like meat, vegetables, toiletry and other necesseties.  Their children are sent to school and the government pay s all expenses needed.  Some are hired to work in drought relief programs. SUMMARY Destitutes are important members of the community therefore; they deserve to be helped so they can live a normal life. They should be treated with dignity and respect. Indi viduals, organisation and the government help them to live better lives.

questions.prompt: Debswana Mining Company - Donated The Mpule Kwelagobe Children`s Centre to care for orphans and other children with problems.
options: Sick people  Keep them company.  Giving the medicine.  Bathe them.  Making sure they eat a balanced diet.  Helping with their chores
Elderly people  Treating them with dignity.  Keeping them company.  Doing their chores.  Reading them newspapers.

Disabled or physically challenged people  Treat them with dignity.  Provide things necessary to make their lives easier.  Guid e someone who is blind.  Push someone who is on a wheelchair.  Reading newspapers to them.

Poor people  Teaching them skills that will enable them to find work or to become self - employed. @TZ 6 of 11 E. Babies  Provide them with love and attention.  Bathe, clothe and feed them.  Provide them with health care.  Protect them from danger.  Teach them new things and the right behaviour.  Play with them. F. Orphans  Provide them with security and protection.  Play with them.  Give them love.  Provide food and clothe s.  Provide a loving home.  Treat them with dignity. REASONS FOR CARING FOR PEOPLE IN NEED It is important to care for people who have special needs as this makes them feel accepted and loved and also helps them to accept their conditions. Some reasons are :  It is morally right to care and help those in need.  To help them cope with situations or problems that they are faced with.  To give them hope in life.  To help them live a better life.  To make them more comfortable.  People with special needs have the same thoughts and feelings as we have, therefore, we must treat them with respect as we treat everyone else. The care giver also benefits by feeling a sense of satisfaction. HOW PEOPLE LIVING WITH HIV/AIDS CAN TAKE CARE OF THEMSELVES It is imperative that HIV+ people take good care of themselves so that they can improve their health and have a strong immunity to fight off infections and other diseases. They can care for themselves by :  Eating a balanced diet.  Exercising regularly.  Have enough sleep and rest.  Having safe and protected sex.  Going for check - up on time.  Taking the r ight medication on time.  Being positive and hopeful about life HOW PEOPLE LIVING WITH HIV/AIDS CAN TAKE CARE OF OTHERS HIV+ people can take care of others by:  Having only one sexual partner.  Using a condom.  Encouraging other to go for HIV test.  Telling other people about their status so that they can protect themselves.  HIV+ pregnant women must enrol in the PMTCT program ( Prevention of Mother To Child Transmission ).  Counselling and advising other sick people.  Educating others on how t o protect themselves from getting infected. VALUES PROMOTED THROUGH HOME BASED CARE People whose illnesses cannot be cured at the hospital are looked after by their families at home through Community Home Based Care (CHBC) support system. The following v alues are promoted:  Love  Kindness  Compassion  Sympathy  Respect  Privacy  Helping  Forgiveness  Sharing When we show these values, we are saying that we believe everyone is important and that they deserve to be loved and respected. @TZ 7 of 11 THE ROLE PLAYED BY RELIGIOUS ORGANISATIONS TO SUPPORT PEOPLE LIVING WITH HIV & AIDS  Religious organisation has built some hosp itals such as the Seventh Day Adventist hospital in Kanye which was built by the Seventh Day Adventist Church; The Deborah Retief Memorial Hospital in Mochudi was set up by the Dutch Reformed Church.  They pray for them in their homes and in hospitals.  They counsel them to help them accept and make peace with their situation.  They counsel the family members of people infected with HIV and AIDS so that they can take care of their sick relatives.  They give them hope and courage by preaching to them and praying for them.  They give them food, clothes and other necessities.  They build homes and hospices where they can be taken care of.  They provide love and home based care for the sick. questions.prompt: ATR - Relatives care for children left by the dead person. PROBLEMS ASSOCIATED WITH ORPHAN - HOOD - Lack of parental love, care, security and protection. - Loss of sense of belonging. - Orphans could lose hope in life. - Emotional trauma due shock brought by the loss. - Relative may take advantage of them and misuse their inheritance. - Lack of guidance. - Children may end up as street kids. - Children ma y become thieves or prostitutes in order to have money to survive . - Older orphans maybe burdened with the responsibility of caring for their younger orphan siblings. - Teenage girls may become pregnant. - They orphans may leave school if there is no one carin g for them. WAYS OF DEALING WITH PROBLEMS ASSOCIATED WITH ORPHAN - HOOD - Adoption: if children are adopted, they can have a home and parents who will guide and take care of them. The government has rules for adoption so that people who adopt orphans know what is expected - Orphanages: The government, non - governmental organisations and individuals have built orphanages to care for orphans. - Extended family : society is encouraged to follow some values of the past whereby the extended families take of orphans with love and compassion. @TZ 10 of 11 - Laws : the government has laws relating to orphans. There should be close monitoring of orphans so that people do not take advantage of them or abuse the. . ADOPTION  Adoption is when a family make a child who is not their biological child part of their family.  Orphaned children are usually adopted. ADVANTAGES OF ADOPTION - It enables orphans to have parents after losing their own. - It enables orphans to feel loved and wanted again. - Orphans will be raised in a loving environment. - Orphans will receive proper guidance and support from their new family. - Protects orphans against acts of abuse. - The child will learn new things. PROBL EMS THAT COULD ARISE WITH ADOPTION - It might take a long time for the child to get used to the new family. - Sometimes the new parents might not treat the adopted child as their own. The parents can make them do all the work. - New parents may adopt the children because they want their property. - Children might behave well towards their new parents because they are not their real parents. - Not getting along with children of the new family. - Feeling isolated and missing their own families. - Having to learn n ew ways of behaving. CONTRIBUTIONS MADE BY DIFFERENT RELIGIONS TOWARDS THE UNDERPRIVILEGED - People are underprivileged when they have to survive with a low standard of living and they do not have what other people have in life. - People who are underprivileged include:  Poor people  Disabled people  Orphans  Street children Religion Contribution

options: Behind the sun Prepared by:L.SIKU MODULE 3 MATTER AND ENERGY Prepared by:L.SIKU TOPIC MATTER OBJECTIVES:  Describ e the three states of matter in terms of volume and shape.  Classify solids as metals or non - metals  Relate the physical properties of common metals to their uses  Relate the physical properties of non - metals to their uses.  List common household chemicals.  Cl assify household chemicals into solids,liquids or gases  State the uses of given household chemicals. Matter is everything that we come across in our lives, like the air you breathe, the clothes you wear, cool drinks – literally everything! Matter is defin ed as anything that has mass and takes up space. Matter is found in 3 major states ; solid, liquid and gas. There are also ones that are less common and they’re called plasma and beam . All matter is made of atoms . Atoms are the smallest particle of matter . The three states of matter. Solids Solids are objects that keep their own shape and do not flow in a given temperature . Solids are composed of atoms packed tightly together . Solids can be different colors and textures , and they can be turned into different shapes Liquids Prepared by:L.SIKU Liquids do not hold their shape at room temperature . They take the shape of the container they are in and they can flow at a given temperature. There i s space between the atoms of a liquid and they move slightly all of the time . Exa mples of liquids are tea , water and blood. Gases Gases are air - like substances that can move around freely or flow to fit a container and they don’t have their own shape. You can put your hand through gases and you won’t feel them. Gases are always moving. There is so much space between the atoms in gas that you can move around in them easily. Gases will take on the shape of their container and can be compressed into a smaller space . Prepared by:L.SIKU Change of State Matter can move from one state to another, but can still be the same substance. A change of state, also called a phase change , is a physical change from one state of matter to another, for example, from solid to liquid or from liquid to gas. By lowering the temperature of water, it can freeze into a solid. By heating water, it can become steam which is a gas . Whether solid, liquid or gas ‐ water is still water. Metals and Non - Metals Solids can be divided into two groups; metals and non - metals . Metals are materials holding or possessing the characteristics of being shiny, hard, fusible, malleable, ductile, et c. Except for mercury, metals are solids at room temperature and pressure. Non – metals are materials not holding the characteristics of metals, means they are not shiny, hard, fusible, malleable, ductile, etc. Nonmetals are typically poor electrical and thermal conductors and don't have a metallic luster. They can be found as solids, liquids, or gases under ordinary conditions. Examples; Metals Non metals  Iron  Uranium  S odium  Aluminum  Calcium  Gold  Nitrogen  Oxygen  Helium  Sulfur  Chlorine  Carbon Prepared by:L.SIKU  Silver  Copper  mercury  Phosphorus  Iodine  Diamond  Graphite The properties of metals and non - metals Description of a property Metals Non - metals Colour Most are shiny Most are d ull Hardness Most are hard Most are soft Strength Most are strong Most are weak Bending Nearly all can bend Most cannot Density High density Mostly low density Hard to melt Mostly yes Mostly easy to melt Make a ringing Mostly yes No Conduct heat well Yes No Conduct electricity Yes No(except carbon) Uses of metals  build things that carry heavy weights  used for jewellery  shiny parts of motorcars  used to make knives or sharp ends of tools for digging  making wire  used for electric cabl es Uses of non - metals  (Coal and wood) Used to produce heat.  (Phosphorus and Sulphur)Used to make heads of matches.  (Diamond)Used to make drills that can cut through the hardest parts Prepared by:L.SIKU STATES OF MATTER QUIZ

questions.prompt: Pull the rubber band tighter. What is the sound like now?  When the rub ber band is pulled tighter it produces a higher note. We say it has a higher pitch.  Pitch of a musical note is how high or low the note is.  We can change the pitch of the sound of a vibrating object by making it vibrate faster or slower.  The faster the vi bration s , the higher the pitch and the slower the vibration s , the lower the pitch.  Strong vibrations produce louder sounds while weaker vibrations produce softer sounds. FORCE A force is a pull or push. KINDS OF FORCES There are many different kinds of forces. a) Muscular force These are forces exerted by people or animals when they use muscles to push or pull. b) Mechanical Force These are forces exerted by machines and some kind of motor or engine is used to push or pull. @Tz 17 of 19 c) Electric force Rubbing ca uses certain things to become electrically charged. These charges exert a force we call an electric force. d) Magnetic force The force between the poles of different magnets is called a magnetic force. The North Pole and South Pole of another magnet at tract while the North Pole of the one will repel the North Pole of the other. e) Elastic force. When certain things are stretched or squeezed they pull or push back. f) Gravitational force The earth attracts everything and makes it hard to lift things up. This is caused by a force called gravity. THE EFFECTS OF FORCE A force can cause changes to an object in the following ways : • It can change the shape of an object @Tz 18 of 19 • It can change the motion of an object • It can change the direction of an object MEASURING FORCE  Force can be measured by something that stretches when it is pulled like a spring scale ( force meter ) or rubber band.  The larger the for ce , the more the spring or the rubber band stretches.
options: L ight that is produced naturally (not made by peo ple)

Li ght that is produced artificially (made by people). NATURAL LIGHT i) The sun - it produces light and heat. ii) Lightning – a very large electric spark in the sky that lasts for a very short time. iii) Fireflies - they produce a flashing light from the back o f their bodies. 1 Firefly @Tz 14 of 19 ARTIFICIAL LIGHT This is light from sources that are made by people. a) Fire and other flames - anything that burns produces light and heat. b) Electric light – an electric current heat up the th in wire which glows so brightly that it produces light and heat. The electric current can be from a battery or from the electric current. LUMIN OUS AND NON - LUMINOUS BODIES a) LUMINOUS BODIES These are objects that produce light. The sun, fire, burning la mp and electric light bulb are luminous bodies. b) NON - LUMINOUS BODIES These are objects that do not produce light . One can see the object because light from another source light shines on it. The moon is a non - luminous body. REFLECTION OF LIGHT When ligh t falls on any surface it se ems to bounce off that surface – almost like a ball will bounce off a wall. This is called reflection . Light is reflected differently by surfaces. For example , smooth surfaces will cause regular reflection while rough surfaces will cause reflected light to be scattered. REGULAR REFLECTION When light falls on a smooth surface like a mirror , it is reflected back in the same way and the rays stay together. @Tz 15 of 19 SCATTERING OF LIGHT Light rays fall on a rough surf ace, they are reflected but they do not stay together. They are scattered. This is called the scattering of light . The scattering of light is also called irregular reflection . SOUND What is sound? Sound is a form of energy that travels in waves. It enters the ears and produces a sensation we call sound. We hear sound through our ears. Some other sources of sound are: a) People talking. b) A bell ringing. c) A car hooting. d) Thunder roaring. e) A tin falling off the shelf. Pleasant and c lear sounds are musical sounds while unpleasant and harsh sounds are noise . What causes sound? Sound is caused by vibrating objects. questions.prompt: Passport A NATIONAL IDENTITY CARD ● This card is known as Omang. ● All citizens of Botswana who are sixteen years old must have Omang. @TZ 17 of 18 A BOTSWANA PASSPORT ● A passport is a document that allows you to travel to other countries. ● The Botswana passport is only given to citizens. RESPONSIBILITIES OF A GOOD CITIZEN ● Protect countries from enemies ● Pay tax ● Respect constitution ● Show love for the country ● Vote during elections ● Participate in national activities e litter picking ● Obey an d uphold laws of the country NATIONAL SYMBOLS OF BOTSWANA ● The National colours ● The National flag ● The coat of Arms ● The National Anthem COLOURS OF NATIONAL FLAG ⮚ SKY BLUE represent water ⮚ BLACK AND WHITE represent equality, unity and harmony among all races. THE COAT OF ARMS The three cog wheels ● The bulls head ● The three wavy blue bands and the word "Pula meaning rain". ● The black and white striped of Zebra. ● The two Zebra and the elephant tusk. ● The head of sorghum. THE THREE COG WHEELS ● They represent industries. ● Botswana's industries such as manufacturing and mining. THE BULLS HEAD ● Represent cattle farming. THE THREE WAVY BLUE BANDS AND THE WORD PULA ● The blue bands represent water. THE BLACK AND WHITE STRIPED OF ZEBRA ● They represent equality and loyal ty of all races. THE TWO ZEBRA AND THE ELEPHANT TUSK ● They represent wildlife. THE HEAD OF SORGHUM ● It represent Agriculture. ● Sorghum is the staple food of most Batswana. PHILOSOPHY OF THE NATIONAL ANTHEM ⮚ It was written by Mr Kgalemang Tumediso Motsete ⮚ The s ong thanks God and ancestors for giving them the land ⮚ It encourages citizens to work together ⮚ It indicates that Botswana is a peaceful country @TZ 18 of 18 PATRIOTISM What is patriotism? ● Patriotism is a feeling of love, repect, devotion and loyalty to one’s country . IMPORTANCE OF PATRIOTISM ⮚ It hepls unite the nation ⮚ Citizens show support to their country ⮚ C itizens solve their disagreement peacefully ⮚ C reates a spirit of helping those in need WAYS OF SHOWING PATRIOTISM ⮚ By respecting human rights ⮚ By respecting the coun try’s national symbols ⮚ By displaying the national flag and wearing national colours during national events ⮚ By learning how our government works to serve the country ⮚ By doing things that benefit the nation e charity PEACE What is peace? This is when ther e is no war and human Rights are respected. questions.prompt: Batswana began buying more guns. PEOPLE WERE CAPTURED OR KILLED ● Some people were forced to Join the groups that captured them. ● Young men became soldiers in the army of the AmaNdebele and Bakololo. ● Other people were killed during the attacks, example, the Bakololo killed Kgosi Makaba of the Bangwaketse. LACK OF PEACE ● People lived in fear because they could be attacked at any time. ● It was not safe to go to the lands and grow crops or to keep their livestock at the cattle post. PEOPLE BECAME POORER ● As people fled from their attackers they left behind their homes, crops and cattle which were then destroyed or taken by the attac kers. COMMUNITIES BROKE UP ● During these wars, many communities had to run away from the groups that were attacking them. ● The Bakwena went to live among the Bangwaketse. @TZ 16 of 18 ● Some Bangwato went to live around the Bakgalagadi. BATSWANA BEGAN BUYING MORE GUYS ● Som e Batswana groups had been defeated by traders who had guns. ● Many dikgosi started buying guns to protect their people. SOME COMMUNITIES BECAME STRONGER ● Groups such as Bangwaketse, Bangwato and Bakwena organised themselves into stronger communities. ● Kgosi Kgari of the Bangwato introduced the kgamelo system. ● The Kgamelo system involved cattle being given by the dikgosi to some of their people in order to gain their support. CITIZENSHIP ● Citizenship means belonging to a country. WAYS OF ACQUIRING CITIZENSHIP IN BOTSWANA ⮚ By birth ⮚ By adoption ⮚ By registration ⮚ By descent ⮚ By naturalisation CITIZEN BY BIRTH ● Its when you were born in Botswana or one of the parents is a motswana CITIZEN BY DESCENT ● Born outside Botswana but your parents are Batswana CITIZEN BY ADO PTION ● A child less than 3 years becomes a motswana on the day he or she is adopted by a citizen of Botswana. CITIZEN BY NATURALISATION ● If you are from other countries and you have lived in Botswana for more than 10 years you are allowed to apply for citiz enship from the government. ● A person who is married to a citizen of Botswana may apply for naturalisation after living in Botswana for at least 5 years. CITIZEN BY REGISTRATION ● Achild who is over 3 years and adopted by a motswana may apply. ● Foreigners wh o worked hard and showed commitment may be given citizenshipo by the president as an honour. WAYS OF IDENTIFYING CITIZENS OF BOTSWANA ⮚ National identity card ⮚ Botswana passport ⮚ Birth certificate ⮚ Drivers license WAYS OF IDENTIFYING A CITIZEN IN BOTSWANA

questions.prompt: The Balete also came from South Africa and settled in Ramotswa. WHY DID THE ANCESTORS OF DIFFERENT ETHNIC GROUPS MOVED TO NEW AREAS. ● Some groups ran aw ay from wars and conflicts. For example, the Bangwato moved from Dithejwane to Shoshong after their Chief Ngwato, quarrelled with his brother Kwena and Ngwaketse. ● Other people moved after the disagree as to who should be the next chief. For example, after Kgosi Mathiba of the Bangwato chose Khama and not Tawana to be the next chief after his death, Tawana and his supporters moved to Ngamiland. They became known as Batawana. ● Some people moved because they wanted to rule themselves. ADVANTAGES OF DIFFERENT E THNIC GROUPS LIVING TOGETHER ● People can share ideas, knowledge and skills. They can learn from each other. ● People get to know and learn to accept cultures that are different from their own. ● A country can use the different cultures to attract tourists. ● It m akes the country a more interesting place to live in. DISADVANTAGES OF DIFFERENT ETHNIC GROUPS LIVING TOGETHER ● Ethnic groups may not be treated equally. This may lead to war and conflicts. ● Some ethnic groups may feel that they are better than others and l ook down up on them. ● The culture of larger or more powerful ethnic groups may replace the culture of smaller or weaker ethnic groups. ● It is difficult for citizens to develop a sense of national identity when they feel that they are loyal to their ethnic gr oups and put their country second. @TZ 12 of 18 A MAP SHOWING DISTRIBUTIONS OF DIFFERENT ETHNIC GROUPS IN BOTSWANA. questions.prompt: She bought a pair of shoes, but __________ was too big. A it B there C t h e y ( 1 ) Use the following pronouns to complete sentences in q uestions 26 to 28. Circle the correct answer. Write positive answers to questions 24 and 25. An example is given below. Use the spaces provided. 6 It was break time at Phatsimo Primary School. Everyone was running about and having fun. Suddenly, the children started shouting. T hey were in the middle of a very strong wind. The wind was making dust spin around the air. The children ran to hide in the classrooms. As quickly as it had come, the wind moved on. The children looked around the playground, there was rubbish everywhere. This rubbish was composed of bits of paper, plastic, plastic bags, grass and even an old bucket. One of the teachers called Mrs Maswabi blew a whistle. The children stood still, it was a sign for them to go to the assembly area. Mrs Maswabi announced at the assembly that the playground was dirty and they were to pick up all the rubbish. This was very tiring and some of the children grumbled. “It is not our fault that there is rubbish all over the playground,” said Lesego, one of the pupils as she bent to pick up a piece of paper. The paper that Lesego pick ed looked strange. It was small and brightly coloured and it had some writing on it. After all the rubbish wa s picked up, Lesego’s friends looked at the piece of paper she had found. They decided to take it to their teacher Mrs Maswabi who told them it was a very va luable stamp. The stamp was reported missing from the Post Office. After lunch, Mrs Maswabi and Lesego took the stamp to the Post Office. They went into an office which was covered with stamps on the wall. They met Mr Morake, who works in the Post Office. He said he was very happy to meet Lesego because she had found a rare stamp. It was a stamp with animal designs. Read the story below and answer questions 29 to 37. 7 At school the next day, Lesego was doing her Maths home work when she was called to Mrs Maswabi’s offi ce. Mr Morake had come to thank Lesego for finding the stamp. He invited Lesego and her classmates to come to the Post Office and see all the interesting stamps. A dog is the cleverest pet you can own. Dogs can be easily trained to do many things. They can look after cattle and sheep. They can chase away thieves and even guide blind people. There are more than one hundred types of dogs. Dogs can be big or small. The y also have different colours and shapes. Bigger dogs need more s pace than smaller dogs. Dogs need a lot of care. You need to spend time with your dog everyday. Dogs need good food to keep them strong, fit and healthy. A dog that is strong and fit is a good hunter. It can cat ch birds and small animals like hares. It can even run after thieves. Walking a dog gives it good exercise. It can be very expensive to look after a dog. Dogs need to be given good food such as meat mixed with dog biscuits, bread and some cooked vegetables. Th ese can cost a lot of money. Also, the puppies or young dogs need to eat about four times everyday. Big dogs can eat just once in a day. Ever y dog need s basic training so it may be easy for it to live with its owner. A dog should walk just behind its owner. It should sit when it is told to do so. It should also come to the owner when it is called. D ogs protect people bu t they also need them as their friends. So, someone with a dog should make sure a dog is not left alone.

One fine day, Mike, tired of not being able to feed his family, decided to leave the village and move to the city where he was certain to earn enough to feed everyone. Along with his family, he left the village for the city. At night, they stopped under a large tree. There was a stream running nearby where they could wash themselves up . He told his sons to clear the area below the tree, he told his wife to fetch water and he instructed his daughters - in - law to make up the fire and started cutting wood from the tree himself. They didn’t know that in the branches of the tree, there was a t hief hiding. He watched as Mike’s family worked together and also noticed that they had nothing to cook. Mike’s wife also thought the same and asked her husband : Everything is ready but what shall we eat?”. Mike raised his hands to heaven and said, “Don’t worry. He is watching all of this from above. He will help us.” The thief got worried as he had seen that the family was large and worked well together. Taking advantage of the fact that they did not know he was hiding in the branches, he decided to make a quick escape. He climbed down safely when they were not looking and ran for his life. But he left behind the bundle of stolen jewels and money which dropped into Mike’s lap. Mike opened it and jumped with joy when he saw what was inside . The family Read the story below and use it to answer questions 28 to 3 6 . 7 gathered all their belongings and returned to the village. But no one in his family was willing to obey his orders. Being a rich family, they were used to having servants all around. So, the one who went to the river to fetch water enjoyed a nice bath. The one, who went to get wood for fire, went off to sleep. Morris’s wife said, “Everything is ready but what shall we eat?” Morris raised his hands and said, “Don’t worry.
